meta.title: Advanced English Grammar Test (C1-C2)
meta.description: A comprehensive test covering advanced English grammar topics at C1 and C2 levels.
meta.info: This test includes 30 questions on inversion, conditionals, cleft sentences, subjunctive, advanced passive, modals, participle clauses, and more.
meta.author: Qwen3.7

data.hint: Choose the correct inverted structure.
data.question: Rarely ___ such a remarkable display of artistic talent.

explanation.text: Negative adverbials at the beginning of a sentence require subject-auxiliary inversion.
examples: Rarely have I seen such beauty.
Never did he complain.

data.hint: Select the appropriate mixed conditional form.
data.question: If she had taken the job offer last year, she ___ in Paris right now.

explanation.text: This is a mixed conditional: past condition (had taken) with a present result (would live).
explanation.formula: If + past perfect, would + base verb
examples: If I had studied harder, I would be a doctor now.
If he hadn't missed the train, he would be here.

data.hint: Identify the correct cleft sentence structure for emphasis.
data.question: ___ was the manager who approved the controversial proposal.

explanation.text: 'It' is used in cleft sentences to emphasize a specific part of the sentence (the manager).
explanation.formula: It + be + emphasized element + relative clause
examples: It was John who broke the window.
It is the environment that we must protect.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb form for the subjunctive mood.
data.question: The board demanded that the CEO ___ immediately.

explanation.text: Verbs of demand, suggest, or recommend are followed by 'that' + subject + base form of the verb (subjunctive).
examples: I suggest that he be present.
They insisted that she stay.

data.hint: Select the correct advanced passive structure.
data.question: The ancient manuscript is believed ___ in the 12th century.

explanation.text: When the action in the passive infinitive happened before the main verb, we use the perfect passive infinitive.
explanation.formula: Subject + passive verb + to have been + past participle
examples: He is said to have been wealthy.
The castle is thought to have been built in 1066.

data.hint: Choose the correct modal verb for past deduction.
data.question: It ___ rained heavily during the night.

explanation.text: 'Must have' + past participle is used for logical deductions about the past with high certainty.
examples: She must have forgotten our meeting.
They must have left already.

data.hint: Identify the correct participle clause.
data.question: ___ the final chapter, she closed the book with a sigh of satisfaction.

explanation.text: The perfect participle ('having' + past participle) is used to show that one action was completed before another began.
examples: Having completed the task, he went home.
Having lived there for years, she knew the city well.

data.hint: Choose the correct relative pronoun with a preposition.
data.question: The company for ___ I work has just announced a merger.

explanation.text: When a preposition precedes the relative pronoun referring to a person, 'whom' must be used, not 'who' or 'that'.
examples: The man with whom I spoke was very helpful.
The project on which we are working is complex.

data.hint: Select the correct article usage (or zero article).
data.question: ___ honesty is a virtue that is highly valued in all cultures.

explanation.text: Abstract nouns used in a general sense take the zero article.
examples: Love is blind.
Knowledge is power.

data.hint: Choose the correct dependent preposition.
data.question: The new policy is entirely compatible ___ our company's core values.

explanation.text: The adjective 'compatible' is followed by the preposition 'with'.
examples: The software is compatible with all devices.
His actions are not compatible with his words.

data.hint: Select the appropriate linking device for concession.
data.question: ___ the numerous unforeseen challenges.

explanation.text: 'Despite' is a preposition and is followed by a noun phrase, whereas 'although' and 'even though' are conjunctions followed by a clause.
examples: Despite the rain, we went out.
She passed the exam in spite of not studying.

data.hint: Choose the correct reported speech transformation.
data.passage: Direct: 'I may attend the conference,' he said.
data.question: Reported: He said that he ___ attend the conference.

explanation.text: In reported speech, 'may' typically changes to 'might' to reflect the backshift in tense.
examples: She said she might be late.
He mentioned that it might rain.

data.hint: Identify the correct future in the past structure.
data.passage: The committee was to have announced the results yesterday, but the decision
data.question: ___ postponed indefinitely.

explanation.text: The simple past passive 'was postponed' correctly states the factual event that interrupted the planned future-in-the-past action.
explanation.formula: was/were to have + past participle, but + simple past
examples: He was to have arrived at noon, but his flight was delayed.
They were to have signed the deal, but the terms changed.

data.hint: Choose the sentence with correct ellipsis.
data.question: She can play the piano better than ___ .

explanation.text: In formal English, the comparative clause retains the auxiliary verb ('I can') rather than using the object pronoun ('me').
examples: He is taller than I am.
She works harder than he does.

data.hint: Select the correct verb pattern.
data.question: I regret ___ you that your application has been unsuccessful.

explanation.text: 'Regret + to infinitive' is used to announce bad news formally. 'Regret + gerund' refers to feeling sorry about a past action.
examples: I regret to inform you that you failed.
I regret telling him the secret.

data.hint: Choose the correct word to complete the noun clause.
data.question: The question remains ___ we can afford to expand the business at this time.

explanation.text: 'Whether' is preferred over 'if' in formal contexts, especially after prepositions or when the clause is the subject/complement.
examples: It depends on whether it rains.
The issue is whether we can proceed.

data.hint: Select the correct concessive structure.
data.question: ___ I admire his dedication, I cannot support his methods.

explanation.text: 'Much as' is a formal concessive conjunction meaning 'although' or 'even though'.
examples: Much as I like her, I disagree with her.
Much as we tried, we failed.

data.hint: Choose the correct quantifier.
data.question: There is ___ evidence to suggest that the treatment is effective.

explanation.text: 'Evidence' is an uncountable noun. 'Scarcely any' correctly modifies uncountable nouns to mean 'almost no'.
examples: There is scarcely any water left.
He has scarcely any experience.

data.hint: Identify the correct double comparative structure.
data.question: ___ you practice, ___ you will become at playing the instrument.

explanation.text: The double comparative structure shows that two things change together.
examples: The harder you work, the more you achieve.
The sooner, the better.

data.hint: Choose the correct phrasal verb.
data.question: The board decided to ___ the meeting until next week due to the CEO's absence.

explanation.text: 'Put off' means to postpone or delay an event.
examples: We had to put off the wedding.
Don't put off studying until the last minute.

data.hint: Select the correct verb form after 'wish'.
data.question: I wish I ___ harder for the exam last semester.

explanation.text: To express regret about a past situation, 'wish' is followed by the past perfect tense.
examples: I wish I had known earlier.
If only she had listened to my advice.

data.hint: Choose the correct verb form.
data.question: It is high time we ___ a decision on this matter.

explanation.text: The expression 'It is high time' is followed by the past simple tense to indicate that something should have been done already.
explanation.formula: It's high time + subject + past simple
examples: It's high time you went to bed.
It's high time we left.

data.hint: Identify the correct inverted structure with 'so'.
data.question: So exhausted ___ that he fell asleep at his desk.

explanation.text: When 'so + adjective' is fronted for emphasis, it triggers subject-auxiliary inversion.
examples: So beautiful was the view that we stayed.
So quickly did he run that he won.

data.hint: Choose the correct concessive structure.
data.question: ___ he was, he managed to finish the marathon.

explanation.text: 'Adjective + as/though + subject + verb' is a formal concessive structure meaning 'although he was tired'.
examples: Young as she is, she is very talented.
Hard though it was, we succeeded.

data.hint: Select the correct tense to emphasize duration before a past event.
data.passage: By the time the rescue team arrived, the climbers
data.question: ___ for three days.

explanation.text: The past perfect continuous (or passive equivalent) emphasizes the duration of an action leading up to another past event.
explanation.formula: had been + past participle (passive) / had been + verb-ing
examples: They had been waiting for hours.
The house had been abandoned for years.

data.hint: Choose the correct causative structure.
data.question: I need to get this document ___ before the meeting starts.

explanation.text: The causative 'get/have + object + past participle' means to arrange for someone else to do something.
examples: I must have my hair cut.
She got her car repaired.

data.hint: Identify the sentence with correct object fronting for emphasis.

explanation.text: Fronting the object to the beginning of the sentence adds emphasis and is grammatically sound in formal or literary English.
examples: That movie I absolutely loved.
Him I do not trust.

data.hint: Choose the appropriate discourse marker.
data.question: ___, we must continue to support it to ensure its success.

explanation.text: 'Be that as it may' is a formal discourse marker used to concede a point but state that it does not change the main argument.
explanation.formula: Be that as it may, + main clause
examples: It's expensive. Be that as it may, we need it.
Be that as it may, the rules must be followed.

data.hint: Select the sentence that best uses nominalization for a formal tone.

A.text: The committee decided to investigate the matter, which caused a delay.

B.text: The committee's decision to investigate the matter caused a delay.

C.text: Because the committee decided to investigate, there was a delay.

D.text: The committee decided on investigating, making a delay happen.

explanation.text: Nominalization (turning verbs/adjectives into nouns) creates a more formal, concise, and academic tone.
examples: The implementation of the policy was swift.
His refusal to cooperate was noted.

data.hint: Choose the correct fixed expression with subjunctive.
data.passage: We will proceed with the launch,
data.question: ___ the potential risks involved.

explanation.text: 'Come what may' is a fixed subjunctive expression meaning 'whatever happens'.
examples: We will stand by our decision, come what may.
He will finish the race, come what may.
